The exact cause of Alzheimer's disease is not yet fully understood [d1][d3][d7][d8]. According to the National Institute on Aging, the causes "probably include a combination of age-related changes in the brain, along with genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors" [d1], a view echoed by the CDC, which states "there likely is not a single cause but rather several factors that can affect each person differently" [d3]. The Alzheimer's Association similarly notes that the disease "likely develops from multiple factors, such as genetics, lifestyle and environment," and has confirmed that aluminum — once suspected — is not a cause [d2]. In the brains of people with Alzheimer's, scientists have found amyloid plaques, neurofibrillary (tau) tangles, and chemical imbalances, but it remains unclear whether these changes cause the disease or result from it [d5][d8]. Harvard Health notes that for roughly 1% of cases, three specific genes are deterministic, while for the remaining 99%, "amyloid and tau are closely associated with Alzheimer's, but many things may contribute to the development of symptoms, such as inflammation in the brain, vascular risk factors, and lifestyle" [d7]. Age is consistently identified as the greatest known risk factor, with risk roughly doubling every five years after age 65 [d1][d2][d6][d8], and Quanta Magazine describes Alzheimer's as "one of the greatest unsolved mysteries of modern medicine" [d4].
